meta.subject: CALCULUS_II
meta.author: bank-team-calculus-2
meta.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.learningObjective: Compute the limit of a convergent sequence
questions.stem: Astronomer Maya logs a_n = (3n+2)/(n+5) and asks for the sequence limit as n grows.
questions.explanation: Divide numerator and denominator by n; the constant terms vanish, leaving 3. A common slip keeps the constants and gets 2/5.
questions.hint: Divide top and bottom by n.

questions.learningObjective: Identify a monotone increasing bounded sequence
questions.stem: In her log, astronomer Leo lists a_n = 1 - 1/n and asks whether it is monotone and bounded.

options.text: It is increasing and bounded above by one.
It is decreasing and bounded below by zero.
It is increasing but unbounded above.
options.misconception: ignores the upper bound of one

options.text: It is neither monotone nor bounded.

questions.explanation: Each term increases toward 1, so it is increasing and bounded above by 1. The tempting error calls it unbounded.

questions.learningObjective: Decide convergence of a geometric series
questions.stem: Astronomer Priya sums 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + ... in her observation log and asks if it converges.

options.text: It diverges because infinitely many terms are added.
It diverges because the ratio equals one half squared.
It converges because the ratio has magnitude less than one.
It converges only if the first term is one.

questions.explanation: A geometric series converges when |r|<1; here r=1/2. The tempting error assumes infinitely many terms force divergence.

questions.learningObjective: Apply the nth-term test for divergence
questions.stem: Astronomer Tom checks a_n = (-1)^n and computes its limit superior minus limit inferior.
questions.explanation: The sequence alternates between -1 and 1, so limsup - liminf = 2. A slip computes only the limsup.

questions.learningObjective: Compute the sum of a convergent geometric series
questions.stem: In his log, astronomer Ken sums 2 + 1 + 1/2 + 1/4 + ... and records the total.
questions.explanation: First term 2, ratio 1/2, so sum = 2/(1-1/2)=4. A common slip uses ratio 1/4.

questions.learningObjective: Sum an alternating geometric series
questions.stem: Astronomer Nia sums 1 - 1/3 + 1/9 - 1/27 + ... and records the total.
questions.explanation: First term 1, ratio -1/3, so sum = 1/(1+1/3)=3/4. A slip forgets the alternating sign.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize a divergent geometric series
questions.stem: Astronomer Ruth asks whether 3 + 6 + 12 + 24 + ... converges in her log.

options.text: It converges to six because terms double.
It diverges because terms are odd.
It converges to three by the first term.
It diverges because the ratio exceeds one in magnitude.

questions.explanation: Ratio r=2, |r|>1, so the series diverges. The tempting error assumes a finite limit exists.

questions.learningObjective: Find the limit of a rational sequence
questions.stem: Astronomer Zoe logs a_n = (2n^2+3)/(n^2+1) and asks for its limit.
questions.explanation: Leading coefficients give 2/1=2. A slip cancels n^2 incorrectly and gets 3.

questions.learningObjective: Convert a repeating decimal to a fraction
questions.stem: Astronomer Ada records 0.333... as a measurement and converts it to a fraction.
questions.explanation: 0.333... = 1/3. The numeric value is one third. A slip rounds to 0.33.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize divergence of the harmonic series
questions.stem: Astronomer Ben asks in his log whether 1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/4 + ... converges.

options.text: It diverges despite terms tending to zero.
It converges because terms tend to zero.
options.misconception: confuses nth term tending to zero with convergence

options.text: It diverges because terms are all positive.
options.misconception: positivity alone does not imply divergence

questions.explanation: Terms tend to zero but the harmonic series still diverges. The tempting error applies the nth-term test incorrectly.
questions.hint: Zero terms are necessary, not sufficient.

questions.learningObjective: Determine whether an oscillating sequence converges
questions.stem: Astronomer Cal asks whether a_n = (-1)^n / n converges in his log.
questions.explanation: The amplitude 1/n tends to zero, so the sequence converges to zero. The tempting error calls all alternating sequences divergent.

questions.learningObjective: Relate bounded partial sums to convergence
questions.stem: Astronomer Dan notes partial sums of a series are bounded and asks what follows.

options.misconception: bounded partial sums alone guarantee convergence
confuses bounded sums with zero terms

questions.explanation: Bounded partial sums alone do not imply convergence; monotonicity is also needed. The tempting error assumes boundedness suffices.

questions.learningObjective: Compute a finite geometric sum
questions.stem: Astronomer Eve computes 1 + 2 + 4 + ... + 2^9 in her log.
questions.explanation: Sum of 2^k for k=0..9 = 2^10 - 1 = 1023. A slip uses 2^9 - 1.

questions.learningObjective: Analyze oscillating partial sums of a series
questions.stem: Astronomer Fay observes partial sums oscillating between -1 and 1 and asks about convergence.

options.text: The series diverges because partial sums do not settle.

questions.explanation: If partial sums do not approach a single value, the series diverges. The tempting error averages the oscillation.

questions.learningObjective: Compute a limit involving a square root
questions.stem: Astronomer Gus logs a_n = sqrt(n^2+n)-n and asks for its limit.
questions.explanation: Rationalize: (n)/(sqrt(n^2+n)+n) -> 1/2. A slip forgets to divide by n.

questions.learningObjective: Apply monotone convergence theorem
questions.stem: Astronomer Hal asks what monotone convergence theorem guarantees for a bounded increasing sequence.

options.text: It guarantees the sequence diverges to infinity.
It guarantees the sequence is constant.
It guarantees convergence to a finite limit.

questions.explanation: A bounded monotone sequence converges to a finite limit. The tempting error assumes unboundedness.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the convergence condition precisely
questions.stem: Astronomer Ivy asks for which ratios a geometric series converges.

options.text: For r greater than zero only.
For r between zero and two.

questions.explanation: Convergence requires |r|<1, including negative ratios. The tempting error uses r<1 without absolute value.

questions.learningObjective: Use nth-term test to show divergence
questions.stem: Astronomer Jay asks what the nth-term test proves when a_n does not tend to zero.

options.text: It proves the terms are positive.

questions.explanation: If terms do not tend to zero, the series diverges. The tempting error thinks the test is inconclusive.
questions.hint: Nonzero limit of terms implies divergence.

questions.learningObjective: Compute sum with a non-integer ratio
questions.stem: Astronomer Kim sums 5 + 5/3 + 5/9 + ... and records the total.

questions.learningObjective: Evaluate an alternating series sum
questions.stem: Astronomer Liv sums 4 - 2 + 1 - 1/2 + ... and records the total.
questions.explanation: a=4, r=-1/2, sum=4/(1+1/2)=8/3. A slip ignores the alternating sign.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why a geometric series diverges
questions.stem: Astronomer Max asks why 1 + 2 + 4 + ... diverges.

options.text: Because the ratio is less than two.

options.misconception: positivity alone does not imply divergence

options.text: Because partial sums grow without bound.
Because there are infinitely many terms.
options.misconception: infinite terms alone do not imply divergence

questions.explanation: Partial sums grow without bound, so no finite limit. The tempting error blames infinite terms.

questions.learningObjective: Handle a rational sequence with higher-degree numerator
questions.stem: Astronomer Nan logs a_n = (n^3+2n)/(2n^3-1) and asks for its limit.
questions.explanation: Leading coefficients 1/2 = 0.5. A slip cancels n^3 and leaves 2/(-1).

questions.learningObjective: Convert 0.123 repeating to a fraction
questions.stem: Astronomer Ora records 0.123123... and converts it to a fraction's decimal value.
questions.explanation: The repeating decimal equals 41/333 ≈ 0.123123. The numeric value is as given. A slip truncates.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish p-series convergence
questions.stem: Astronomer Pat asks whether sum 1/n^2 converges.

options.text: It diverges like the harmonic series.
It diverges because terms are positive.
It converges because p exceeds one.

questions.explanation: A p-series converges when p>1. The tempting error compares it to the harmonic series.

questions.learningObjective: Identify bounded oscillation without convergence
questions.stem: Astronomer Qin asks about a_n = sin(n) in her log.

options.text: It is bounded but does not converge.

questions.explanation: sin(n) stays in [-1,1] but never settles. The tempting error assumes bounded implies convergent.

questions.learningObjective: Combine bounded partial sums with terms tending to zero
questions.stem: Astronomer Rae asks if bounded partial sums plus terms tending to zero guarantee convergence.
questions.explanation: Monotone convergence needs monotonicity; bounded sums plus zero terms are not enough. The tempting error assumes sufficiency.

questions.learningObjective: Compute a finite geometric sum with ratio one half
questions.stem: Astronomer Sam computes 1/2 + 1/4 + ... + 1/2^8 in his log.

questions.learningObjective: Compute Cesaro average of oscillating partial sums
questions.stem: Astronomer Tara averages the first four partial sums -1,1,-1,1 and records the mean.
questions.explanation: Average = (-1+1-1+1)/4 = 0. A slip sums without dividing.

questions.learningObjective: Compute limit of exponential over polynomial
questions.stem: Astronomer Uma logs a_n = 2^n / n^2 and asks for its limit.
questions.explanation: Exponential dominates polynomial, so the limit is infinity; recorded as a large value. A slip treats it as zero.

questions.learningObjective: Show a sequence is decreasing and bounded
questions.stem: Astronomer Vera checks a_n = (n+1)/n and asks its monotonicity.

options.text: It is decreasing and bounded below by one.
It is increasing and bounded below.

questions.explanation: (n+1)/n = 1 + 1/n decreases to 1. The tempting error sees n+1 and calls it increasing.

questions.learningObjective: Compute common ratio from terms
questions.stem: Astronomer Will logs terms 6, -3, 3/2 and computes the common ratio.
questions.explanation: Ratio = -3/6 = -1/2. A slip uses 3/(-3) = -1.

questions.learningObjective: Apply nth-term test to a trigonometric term
questions.stem: Astronomer Xan asks whether sum sin(n) converges by the nth-term test.

options.text: It converges because sin(n) is bounded.
It diverges because sin(n) is positive.
The test is inconclusive since sin(n) has no limit.
It converges to the average of sin.

questions.explanation: sin(n) has no limit, so the nth-term test gives no conclusion. The tempting error assumes bounded terms suffice.
questions.hint: Need the term limit to be zero.

questions.learningObjective: Compute sum of an alternating geometric series
questions.stem: Astronomer Yve sums 10 - 5 + 5/2 - 5/4 + ... and records the total.

questions.learningObjective: Identify convergence of an alternating geometric series
questions.stem: Astronomer Zed asks whether 1 - 2 + 4 - 8 + ... converges.

options.text: It diverges because terms are negative.

questions.explanation: |r|=2>1, so it diverges. The tempting error assumes alternating implies convergence.

questions.learningObjective: Compute partial sum growth rate
questions.stem: Astronomer Abe records partial sum S_5 of 1+2+4+... and its value.

questions.learningObjective: Handle denominator of higher degree
questions.stem: Astronomer Bea logs a_n = (3n+1)/(n^2+2) and asks for its limit.
questions.explanation: Denominator degree higher, so limit 0. A slip compares constants 3/2.

questions.learningObjective: Convert 0.5 repeating to a fraction
questions.stem: Astronomer Cal records 0.555... and converts it to a fraction's decimal value.
questions.explanation: 0.555... = 5/9 ≈ 0.555556. The numeric value is as given. A slip uses 1/2.

questions.learningObjective: Apply integral test idea to harmonic series
questions.stem: Astronomer Dan asks why the integral test shows harmonic series diverges.
questions.explanation: The integral of 1/x diverges, so the series diverges. The tempting error reverses the integral result.

questions.learningObjective: Compute limit of damped oscillation
questions.stem: Astronomer Eli logs a_n = cos(n)/n and asks for its limit.
questions.explanation: Bounded numerator over growing denominator tends to zero. A slip says cos has no limit.

questions.learningObjective: Relate bounded partial sums to absolute convergence
questions.stem: Astronomer Fay asks if bounded partial sums imply absolute convergence.

options.text: Yes, bounded partial sums imply absolute convergence.
No, absolute convergence needs sum of |a_n| bounded.

questions.explanation: Absolute convergence requires bounded partial sums of |a_n|. The tempting error confuses conditional convergence.

questions.learningObjective: Compute finite geometric sum with first term not one
questions.stem: Astronomer Gus computes 3 + 6 + 12 + ... + 3*2^4 in his log.

questions.learningObjective: Determine convergence from partial sum pattern
questions.stem: Astronomer Hal sees partial sums 0,1,0,1,... and asks about convergence.

options.text: It diverges because no single limit.

questions.explanation: No single limit exists, so divergence. The tempting error averages the two values.

questions.learningObjective: Compute limit of a_n = n/(n+1)
questions.stem: Astronomer Ivy logs a_n = n/(n+1) and asks for its limit.
questions.explanation: Divide by n: 1/(1+1/n) -> 1. A slip keeps 1/(n+1).
questions.hint: Divide numerator and denominator by n.

questions.learningObjective: Apply boundedness to a decreasing sequence
questions.stem: Astronomer Jay asks what a bounded decreasing sequence does.

options.text: It converges to a finite limit.

questions.explanation: Bounded decreasing sequence converges. The tempting error assumes unboundedness.

questions.learningObjective: Test convergence at boundary ratio
questions.stem: Astronomer Ken asks whether a geometric series with r = -1 converges.
questions.explanation: |r|=1, so terms do not tend to zero and it diverges. The tempting error applies the sum formula.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize inconclusive nth-term test
questions.stem: Astronomer Liv asks what happens when terms tend to zero.
questions.explanation: Terms tending to zero is necessary but not sufficient; the test is inconclusive. The tempting error assumes convergence.

questions.learningObjective: Compute sum with ratio -1/3
questions.stem: Astronomer Max sums 9 - 3 + 1 - 1/3 + ... and records the total.

questions.learningObjective: Compute alternating sum with ratio -2/3
questions.stem: Astronomer Nan sums 6 - 4 + 8/3 - 16/9 + ... and records the total.

questions.learningObjective: Identify divergence of a geometric series
questions.stem: Astronomer Ora asks whether 5 + 10 + 20 + ... converges.

options.text: It diverges because terms are even.

questions.explanation: r=2, |r|>1, so divergence. The tempting error assumes a finite sum.

questions.learningObjective: Compute limit with equal degrees and leading coeff
questions.stem: Astronomer Pat logs a_n = (4n^2-1)/(2n^2+3) and asks for its limit.
questions.explanation: Leading coeff ratio 4/2=2. A slip uses constants -1/3.

questions.learningObjective: Convert 0.27 repeating to a fraction
questions.stem: Astronomer Qin records 0.2727... and converts it to a fraction's decimal value.
questions.explanation: 0.2727... = 3/11 ≈ 0.272727. The numeric value is as given. A slip truncates.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize divergence of a harmonic-like series
questions.stem: Astronomer Rae asks whether sum 1/(2n) converges.

options.misconception: confuses sum with limit of terms

options.text: It diverges as a scaled harmonic series.
It diverges because terms are odd.

questions.explanation: Scaling harmonic series by 1/2 still diverges. The tempting error assumes halving terms converges.
questions.hint: Constant multiple of divergent series diverges.

questions.learningObjective: Compute limit of (-1)^n/n^2
questions.stem: Astronomer Sam logs a_n = (-1)^n/n^2 and asks for its limit.
questions.explanation: Amplitude 1/n^2 -> 0, so limit 0. A slip says oscillation prevents convergence.

questions.learningObjective: Identify a series with bounded partial sums
questions.stem: Astronomer Tara asks which series has bounded partial sums.
questions.explanation: Alternating harmonic has bounded partial sums. The tempting error picks harmonic.

questions.learningObjective: Compute finite sum with ratio 3
questions.stem: Astronomer Uma computes 1 + 3 + 9 + 27 in her log.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize non-convergence from unbounded oscillation
questions.stem: Astronomer Vera sees partial sums grow in magnitude while alternating sign.

options.text: It diverges because partial sums unbounded.

options.misconception: conditional convergence requires bounded partial sums

questions.explanation: Unbounded partial sums imply divergence. The tempting error assumes cancellation.

questions.learningObjective: Compute limit of n-th root of n
questions.stem: Astronomer Will logs a_n = n^(1/n) and asks for its limit.
questions.explanation: n^(1/n) -> 1. A slip says it grows to infinity.

questions.learningObjective: Identify a sequence that is not monotone
questions.stem: Astronomer Xan asks whether a_n = (-1)^n / n is monotone.
questions.explanation: The sequence alternates sign, so not monotone. The tempting error focuses on magnitude.

questions.learningObjective: Compute common ratio from a word problem
questions.stem: Astronomer Yve logs a geometric series 8,4,2,... and computes its ratio.
questions.explanation: Ratio = 4/8 = 1/2. A slip uses 2/4 = 1/2? Actually correct. A common slip uses 8/4=2.

questions.learningObjective: Apply nth-term test to a rational term
questions.stem: Astronomer Zed asks whether sum n/(n+1) converges by the nth-term test.

options.text: It converges because terms are less than one.

options.misconception: terms actually increase to one but reason is nonzero limit

options.text: It diverges because terms tend to one.

questions.explanation: Terms tend to 1, not zero, so divergence. The tempting error assumes terms <1 suffice.
